normalized.governing_thought: Recommendation: do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027. Put the money into the software business, which can break even within today's cash if growth holds
executive_summary: Orders lose money at every level of performance we have seen. At the median of the 14 customer sites our software runs, each order loses $2.67 before dark-store costs and $6.17 after them. Combining the best value seen at any site on every input, which no single site has managed, still loses $1.76.

The founders' plan turns positive only by beating our best site on three drivers at once. It assumes a $45 order (best seen: $42), 3.5 orders per rider-hour (best: 3.0), 1,800 orders a day (best: 1,400) and promotions at 2% of order value (every site: 6%). If order value or rider productivity only reaches the median, orders lose money again.

Our own test and the market point the same way. The Columbus pop-up lost about $12.57 per order, falling below the median on every driver, and only 22% of customers were still ordering in month three. Both incumbents lose money on every order; QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

The plan breaks the 12-month runway rule even if it works; the software path does not. Holding 12 months of runway leaves $7.2M to deploy, and the plan needs $9.5M. Adding $0.8M a year of engineering and sales reaches break-even in months 26–32 if growth holds at 45–60% and other costs stay flat.

Decisions we ask the board to take: 1. Decline Parcelbird Now for 2027. 2. Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to work the 37-grocer pipeline. 3. Ask management to package the software for grocers who want fast delivery from their own stores, selling to that trend rather than competing with our pipeline. 4. Agree now what would reopen the question (page 12).

slides.title: Of the founders' four claims, only market growth holds up, and the plan fails both of the board's constraints

claims.claim: “Quick commerce is growing over 40% a year” — Supported
evidence: US quick-commerce grocery sales rose from $1.8B (2022) to $5.1B (2025), or 41.5% a year compounded.

claims.claim: “Nobody owns the Midwest” — Partly
evidence: No operator is named as owning it.
the one regional operator, QuickBasket, loses $3.40 per order and closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025; an open market may simply be an unprofitable one.

claims.claim: “We know how to run them better than anyone” — Not shown
evidence: Our six-week Columbus pop-up was below our customers' median on all four drivers: order value $31 vs $34, promotions 12% vs 6%, 2.1 vs 2.4 orders per rider-hour, 280 vs 900 orders a day.
Six weeks is early, but order value and promotions depend little on ramp-up.

claims.claim: “Contribution profit per order by month 18” — Not supported
evidence: Requires order value, rider productivity and store density all above the best of the 14 sites at once, and promotions at one-third of the benchmark (pages 5–7).

claims.claim: Path to profitability within current cash — Fails
evidence: At benchmark-median performance a mature dark store loses about $2.0M a year, so nine would lose about $18M a year, more than the $12.0M we hold.
A new round is “unlikely”.

claims.claim: At least 12 months of runway at all times — Fails
evidence: The plan needs $9.5M to month 18; only $7.2M is available above a 12-month reserve (page 9).

slides.title: The market is growing about 40% a year, yet both incumbent operators lose money on every order

claims.claim: US quick-commerce grocery GMV grew 41.5% a year compounded, 2022–25
evidence: 2023: $2.6B (+44% vs prior year)
2024: $3.6B (+38% vs prior year)
2025: $5.1B (+42% vs prior year)

claims.claim: Both incumbent operators lose money on every order
evidence: Zipcart (national): revenue $1,200M; EBITDA −$310M; EBITDA margin −26%; contribution per order −$1.90
QuickBasket (regional): revenue $210M; EBITDA −$96M; EBITDA margin −46%; contribution per order −$3.40
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities in 2025.

claims.claim: Demand is not the question. Growth has not produced profit: the larger operator loses less per order than the regional one, but neither covers its costs. The board's question is whether any operator, including us, can make money on each order.

slides.title: Only the founders' plan earns money per order, and it assumes better-than-best performance on every driver

claims.claim: Per-order economics by scenario
evidence: Columbus pop-up (6 weeks, autumn 2026): $31; 12%; 2.1; 280; before store costs −$6.21; store cost −$6.36; after store costs −$12.57
Benchmark median (our 14 customer sites, 2025): $34; 6%; 2.4; 900; −$2.67; −$3.50; −$6.17
Best seen on every input (no site achieved all at once): $42; 6%; 3.0; 1,400; +$0.49; −$2.25; −$1.76
▲ = beyond the best value seen at any of the 14 sites (promotions: below the 6% every site ran)

claims.claim: Even the best-of-everything case loses $1.76 per order once a store's $1.15M annual cost is spread across 1,400 orders a day.
evidence: Adding the plan's 2% promotions only reaches break-even (−$0.08).

claims.claim: The benchmark looks representative
evidence: our median, −$2.67 before store costs, sits between the incumbents' reported −$1.90 and −$3.40 per order.

claims.claim: The pop-up's store cost per order is inflated by low volume (280 orders a day), but it also lost $6.21 per order before any store cost.
evidence: Pop-up store cost uses its annualised $650K fixed cost.
Best order value and best density came from different sites.

slides.title: Closing the $8.19 gap between the median and the plan takes four improvements at once; order value and rider productivity supply over half

claims.claim: Waterfall from benchmark median (−$6.17) to founders' plan (+$2.02)
evidence: Order value $34 → $45 (best seen: $42): +$2.31
Promotions 6% → 2% (every site: 6%): +$1.80
Rider productivity 2.4 → 3.5 / hour (best seen: 3.0): +$2.32
Store density 900 → 1,800 / day (best seen: 1,400): +$1.75
Steps are calculated in the order shown: the order-value step is valued at 6% promotions, the promotion step at a $45 order. Figures may not sum because of rounding.

claims.claim: Order value +32% over the median and $3 above the best site, without losing the convenience use case (a risk the pack itself flags).
Promotions at a third of the benchmark.
evidence: The pop-up ran at 12%, twice the benchmark.

claims.claim: Rider productivity 17% above the best site, outside the observed 1.9–3.0 range.
Density 29% above the best site, outside the 400–1,400 range.
evidence: The pop-up averaged 280 a day.

slides.title: The plan has no room for error: if order value or rider productivity stays at the median, every order loses money

claims.claim: If one plan input falls back to the benchmark median (contribution after store costs)
evidence: Founders' plan as proposed: +$2.02
Density at 900 orders a day: +$0.27
Promotions at 6%: +$0.22
Rider productivity at 2.4 / hour: −$0.31
Order value at $34: −$0.73

claims.claim: Only 3 of 16 combinations of plan and median inputs make money
evidence: Rows (order value / rider productivity at plan) × columns (promotions / density at plan: Neither, Plan promotions, Plan density, Both)
Plan rider productivity: −$3.84, −$2.48, −$2.09, −$0.73

claims.claim: All three profitable cases need both the $45 order and 3.5 orders per rider-hour, and each is above the best site we have seen.
Rider pay rules add downside
evidence: Two of the three target cities are considering minimum pay for delivery workers.
Each extra $1 per rider-hour costs $0.29 per order at plan productivity ($0.42 at the median); $7.06 more an hour (+40%) erases the plan's margin on its own.

claims.claim: Even with all four plan inputs, the margin is thin
evidence: $2.02 is 4.5% of a $45 order.

slides.title: Demand is thinner than the survey suggests: 22% of pop-up customers stayed, so each retained customer cost about $173 to acquire

claims.claim: Stated intent vs observed behaviour
evidence: 44% of 1,500 Columbus residents aged 25–39 said they would use 15-minute delivery at least weekly
22% of pop-up customers were still ordering in month three
3.1 orders a month from those who stayed: less than once a week
$173 to acquire each customer who stays ($38 acquisition cost ÷ 22%)

claims.claim: Payback on acquisition depends entirely on per-order economics
evidence: Pop-up actual, after store costs (−$12.57): −$38.97 per retained customer per month; never recovers $173
Benchmark median, after store costs (−$6.17): −$19.12; never
Founders' plan, before store costs (+$3.77): +$11.68; ≈15 months
Founders' plan, after store costs (+$2.02): +$6.26; ≈28 months
Contribution = 3.1 orders × per-order result. Ignores orders in months 1–3 and any later churn.

claims.claim: It is an early read.
evidence: One temporary site for six weeks; orders grew 18% a week, which implies an exit rate of roughly 410 a day if growth was steady. That is still under half the 900 median.

claims.claim: The growth was bought.
evidence: Promotions averaged 12% of order value, and each customer cost $38 in paid social and first-order credits.

claims.claim: One figure needs checking.
evidence: A six-week test cannot fully observe month-three retention, so management should confirm how the 22% was measured.

slides.title: Even if every assumption holds, the plan breaks the board's rule of keeping 12 months of runway

claims.claim: Cash available vs. cash the plan needs
evidence: Cash in the bank today $12.0M: available $7.2M, 12-month reserve $4.8M
Plan's cash need to month 18 (founders' figure): $9.5M
Plan's need if today's software burn ($7.2M over 18 months) comes on top: $16.7M
Reserve = 12 months × today's $0.4M monthly burn, the most lenient test.

claims.claim: Even on the founders' own figure, the plan needs $2.3M more than can be spent without breaching the reserve.
At best, $2.5M left at month 18.
evidence: That is about 6 months of runway even at today's burn. With even spending, runway falls below 12 months around month 11.

claims.claim: If the $9.5M excludes today's burn, cash runs out around month 13.
evidence: That is before the plan's own month-18 milestone.

claims.claim: The $9.5M already assumes the plan's economics.
evidence: At benchmark-median performance each mature store loses about $2.0M a year, so nine would lose about $18M a year.

claims.claim: There is no backstop.
evidence: The lead investor calls a new round for a delivery operator “unlikely in this market”.

slides.title: Of three options, only scaling the software business meets both of the board's constraints

claims.claim: A. Launch Parcelbird Now as proposed (9 dark stores in 3 cities; $5.4M capex; $9.5M to month 18)
evidence: Per-order economics: Fails — Positive only with better-than-best inputs: +$2.02 in the plan, −$6.17 at the median.
Cash and 12-month runway: Fails — Needs $9.5M against $7.2M available above the 12-month reserve.
Path to profit within current cash: Fails — None at any performance we have observed.
Effect on core software business: Fails — Makes us a competitor to grocers in our pipeline and splits management attention.

claims.claim: B. Open one permanent Columbus store as a further test ($0.6M capex plus one store's operating losses)
evidence: Per-order economics: Fails — Same economics at small scale: about −$2.0M a year per store at the median.
Cash and 12-month runway: Partly — About $2.6M in year one fits, but uses the cushion the software plan relies on.
Path to profit: Fails — None; delays the software break-even.
Effect on core: Partly — Smaller conflict, but repeats what the pop-up and the 14-site benchmark already show.

claims.claim: C. Scale software; serve grocers' own fast delivery ($0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires) — RECOMMENDED
evidence: Per-order economics: Meets — Software at 81% gross margin; no exposure to per-order losses.
Cash and 12-month runway: Meets — Cash bottoms at $3.6–5.4M at 45–60% growth; runway stays above 12 months.
Path to profit: Conditional — Break-even in months 26–32 if growth stays ≥45% and other costs are held (page 11).
Effect on core: Meets — Sells to the trend: several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores.

slides.title: Scaling the software business breaks even within today's cash if growth stays at 45% or more and other costs are held

claims.claim: Cash balance by month under three growth rates for software ARR
evidence: 60% a year (today's rate): low $5.4M, month 25; $16.3M at end of chart
45% a year: low $3.6M, month 31; $7.4M at end of chart
30% a year: cash ≈ $0 by month 45

Illustrative Parcelbird model: $12.0M cash and $4.1M ARR in January 2027; revenue = ARR; 81% gross margin; operating costs held at today's implied $8.1M a year (gross profit + $4.8M burn) plus $0.8M for new hires; growth is net of churn. Not a substitute for a bottom-up plan.

claims.claim: The pipeline can support the growth
evidence: 37 grocers in the pipeline, 9 at the late stage, at an average $96,000 a year.
Late-stage deals alone add $0.86M of ARR (+21%); the whole pipeline would add $3.55M (+87%).
Growing 60% in 2027 means about $2.5M of new ARR, roughly 26 contracts at $96,000, net of churn.
Several pipeline grocers want fast delivery from their own stores, which needs the inventory, picking and dispatch tools we already sell.

claims.claim: Cost discipline matters as much as growth
evidence: If other costs rise 10% a year, 60% growth still breaks even (month 32, low of $3.1M), but 45% growth runs out of cash.
At 30% growth, runway falls below 12 months from month 23 even with costs held flat.

slides.title: We ask the board to decline Parcelbird Now for 2027, back a software-led plan, and agree in advance what would reopen the question

claims.claim: Decide in January
evidence: Decline Parcelbird Now for 2027. No dark stores, no capex.
Approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires.
Adopt a runway floor of 12 months, reported at every board meeting against a monthly plan.
Mandate a fast-delivery-from-store offer for pipeline grocers.

claims.claim: Next 90 days (management)
evidence: Put the new sales hires on the 9 late-stage grocers ($0.86M of ARR).
Scope the store-based offer with 3–5 pipeline grocers who want fast delivery.
Finance to replace page 11 with a bottom-up operating plan, with cost growth explicit.
Close the pop-up and confirm how month-three retention was measured.

claims.claim: Reopen the operator question only if all three hold
evidence: A dark store in our customer network covers its own costs (positive after store costs) for two consecutive quarters. Today even the best combined inputs give −$1.76 per order.
Rider minimum-pay rules in the target cities are settled, and the economics re-tested at the new rate.
Software is at break-even, so any venture can be funded without touching the 12-month reserve.

claims.claim: What we give up: A possible first-mover position in Midwest quick commerce. we judge that position to be worth less than the cash and focus it would cost.
evidence: With QuickBasket retreating and Zipcart still losing $1.90 per order at $1.2B of revenue

slides.title: How we handled gaps in the briefing pack, and what management should confirm

claims.claim: Two contribution measures shown because the pack does not define the founders' or incumbents' “contribution per order”.
evidence: “Before store costs” covers every per-order cost; “after store costs” also spreads each dark store's fixed cost over its orders.

claims.claim: The $9.5M plan figure: the pack does not say whether it includes today's $0.4M a month burn, so page 9 shows both readings. The conclusion holds under either.
Runway = cash ÷ current monthly burn. We test the reserve at today's burn, the most lenient basis.
Timing. The $12.0M is treated as cash available in January 2027; the pack does not date it.
Software path (page 11) is a top-down illustration with stated assumptions, not a forecast.
Pop-up exit rate of about 410 orders a day assumes steady 18% weekly growth across the six weeks
evidence: 11,800 orders in total

claims.claim: Waterfall (page 6) is sequential. A different order changes the step sizes, not the end points.
The pack labels its company, competitor and market figures as synthetic benchmark data. No external research was used.

normalized.recommendation: Decline Parcelbird Now for 2027 (no dark stores, no capex); approve $0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires to work the 37-grocer pipeline; adopt a runway floor of 12 months, reported at every board meeting against a monthly plan; mandate (package the software for) a fast-delivery-from-store offer for pipeline grocers; and agree now what would reopen the question.

alternatives_considered.option: C. Scale software; serve grocers' own fast delivery ($0.8M a year for 2 engineers and 2 sales hires)
